## Methods

Data collection
We constructed a global database to jointly investigate how SOC responses are influenced by changes in plant and soil microbial diversity to N enrichment, adhering to the PRISMA guidelines88 (Preferred Reporting Items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses) (Supplementary Fig. 9). Peer-reviewed publications on the impacts of N enrichment on plant and soil microbial diversity in our study were searched using the Web of Science (https://webofscience.clarivate.cn/wos/woscc/basic-search) and China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI, https://www.cnki.net), including all research up to April 1, 2023 (a full list is provided in Supplementary Data 1). Keywords used were: “(nitrogen fertilization OR N deposition OR nitrogen addition OR N enrichment) AND (plant OR soil microbial) AND (richness) AND (SOC OR MBC OR plant biomass)”. We focused on diversity and biomass of plant and soil microbes as: (1) there is a significant knowledge gap regarding how their responses affect carbon allocation between plant and soil microbial biomass, and thus soil C storage under N enrichment; and (2) to provide a balanced dataset that considers both plant and soil microbes, as these variables are rarely measured simultaneously in studies.

Relevant publications were selected based on the following criteria: (1) N fertilizer was directly applied to terrestrial ecosystems under field conditions using paired treatment-control plots, excluding laboratory incubation studies. (2) At least one soil microbial phylotype related to diversity (richness), including bacteria and fungi, or biomass (MBC) was reported. (3) N application rate and experiment duration were recorded to standardize the effect of N enrichment across studies. (4) Means and sample sizes for the selected variables were available or could be calculated from the publications. Our search yielded a dataset of 2141 observations from 275 peer-reviewed studies (Fig. 1a, b), encompassing plant diversity and biomass, soil microbial diversity and biomass, SOC content, and associated climate and soil variables (Supplementary Table 1).

Extracted data
We collected plant and multiple soil variables, including plant species richness and biomass, soil microbial diversity and biomass, soil properties, and SOC from the selected publications. Numerical data were extracted from text, tables, figures, and appendices, whereas graphical data were digitized using GetData Graph Digitizer (http://getdata-graph-digitizer.com). Mean values, standard deviations (SD), and sample sizes (n) were recorded or calculated. When studies reported standard error (SE), it was converted to SD: SD=SE×√n. Climatic variables, including MAT and MAP, were obtained from Worldclim 2.0 (http://www.worldclim.org) based on study coordinates. Ecosystem types were categorized as farmland, forest, and grassland, and climatic regions as tropical (tropical and subtropical), temperate, and polar (polar and boreal), following the 2010 Global Ecological Zones dataset (https://data.apps.fao.org/). Here, we used richness (that is, the number of species) as a metric of diversity, as richness is the most used and simplest89,90. Accordingly, only studies reporting microbial richness were included. Due to prevalent monoculture practices in farmlands, land diversity data were largely unavailable and therefore not included. Soil microbial biomass was represented by MBC91. Soil properties (e.g., pH and moisture), nutrients (e.g., total N, total P, available N, and available P) and SOC were collected in the dataset. Detailed descriptions of all variables are provided in Supplementary Table 1. Since the analytical data were transformed into response ratios for subsequent analyses, any method-induced differences are considered negligible.

Data analyses
In this study, the natural logarithmic response ratio (lnRR), an effect size metric widely applied in meta-analysis, was used to evaluate the effect of N enrichment on each variable. The lnRR of an observation was calculated as follows:

lnRR=ln(XT/XC) (1)

Where XT and XC represent the mean values of response variables in the N treatment (T) and control (C), respectively. The N effect on soil pH was calculated as the difference between the treatment and control groups, as soil pH uses a logarithmic scale.

The weighted mean response ratio (lnRR) for each group (e.g., ecosystem types, climatic regions) was calculated as follows:

lnRR=∑(wi* ×lnRRi)/∑wi* (2)

where m represents the number of observations in group, and wi* is the weighting factor of the ith observation in the group. The wi* was calculated as follows:

wi* = 1/vi* (3)

where vi* is the variance of study (i) in the group. The vi* was calculated as follows:

vi* = vi + T2 (4)

where vi is the within-study variance of study (i), and T2 is the between-studies variance. The vi was calculated as follows:

vi = (SDT2 / (nT XT2)) + (SDC2 / (nC XC2)) (5)

where SDT and SDC are the SD of the variables in the treatment and control treatments, respectively; nT and nC are the sample size in the treatment and control, respectively.

The SE of lnRR was calculated as follows:

s(lnRR)=√1/∑wi* (6)

The 95% CI for lnRR was calculated as follows:

95% CI=lnRR±1.96s(lnRR) (7)

If the 95% CI does not overlap zero, the overall effect size of the N enrichment was significant92. For easier interpretation, the lnRR was back-transformed and expressed as a percentage change (%):

Effect size (%) = (exp(lnRR)−1)×100% (8)

A mixed-effects model was employed to calculate the weighted mean of lnRR using the rma.mv function of the R package metafor93, with lnRR ID nested within study ID as the random effect. The distributions of lnRR for each variable analyzed in this study are presented in Supplementary Figs. 10 and 11. All statistical analyses were performed in R version 4.2.1.

Random forest model
We used random forest analysis to identify the primary predictors of plant and soil microbial diversity, biomass, and SOC responses94. Initially, we analyzed various environmental and biological variables to determine the key drivers of richness in plants, soil bacteria, and fungi. Given the pivotal role of diversity in influencing biomass, we incorporated diversity metrics into the original variables to identify the strongest predictors of plant and microbial biomass responses. Finally, we combined all environmental and biological variables, as well as diversity and biomass metrics from plants and soil microbial communities, to identify the main predictors of SOC response. The random forest models were implemented using the R package spatialRF95, which effectively reduces multicollinearity, captures key variable interactions, and evaluates model robustness through spatial cross-validation94. Before model fitting, we minimized multicollinearity by performing two steps: (1) correlation-based filtering (auto_cor function, |r|>0.6) to remove highly correlated predictors, and (2) variance inflation factor filtering (auto_vif function, VIF>2.5) to further exclude N-induced collinear variables. Predictor importance was assessed by measuring the average decrease in prediction accuracy (mean square error) when the data for a given predictor were permuted across trees.

Due to the uneven distribution of data when incorporating both aboveground and belowground variables, and the inability of the random forest model to handle missing values, we included observations with at least seven available variables in the dataset used to identify key predictors96. This approach ensured robust representation and analytical reliability across all study observations (Supplementary Figs. 12 and 13). To accommodate missing data, values were imputed using the missForest function from the missForest package with the parameter ntree set to 99997.

Mixed-effects meta regression
Mixed-effects meta-regression models were used to examine the relationships between climatic and soil factors (identified through the random forest model) and plant, soil microbial communities, and SOC, using the rma.mv function in the R package metafor92. All models were fitted using inverse-variance weighting to account for differential contributions of each study98. Study ID was included as a random factor, and to account for potential non-independence among response variables arising from shared variance related to N enrichment, N rate level was also included as a random effect.

Threshold identification
In this study, we applied a two-step procedure based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) to identify the most suitable model describing the relationship between the response of soil factors, diversity and biomass or SOC (y) and N enrichment rates (x), followed by previous studies42,43. First, we fitted linear and nonlinear models, including quadratic regressions (simple nonlinear trends) and generalized additive models (GAM, flexible trends using smoothing parameters)42,43. The linear model served as the null hypothesis, representing a gradual x-y relationship. Lower AIC values for nonlinear models indicated a threshold point, suggesting a departure from linear trends. In the second step, thresholds were tested only when nonlinear models demonstrated a better fit. Thresholds were categorized as either continuous or discontinuous. A continuous threshold marks a point of gradual slope change, often identified using GAM or segmented regressions, which capture points of maximum curvature. In contrast, discontinuous thresholds involve abrupt changes in both slope and intercept and are best modeled using step regressions or stegmented regressions (a combination of step and segmented approaches). Among segmented, step, and stegmented regressions, the model with the lowest AIC value was selected. If GAM was the best model, the segmented regression threshold was reported to highlight the point of maximum curvature. To ensure robustness, we removed outliers using the Mahalanobis distance method (cutoff > 12) and restricted threshold searches to the 0.05–0.95 quantile range of x43. Each case underwent 1000 bootstrap resamplings to estimate plausible thresholds, with the mean threshold reported as the final value. We tested the significance of thresholds by bootstrapping linear regressions on either side of the threshold and comparing slopes using a two-sided Mann–Whitney U-test. Threshold detection revealed significant differences in slopes in nearly all cases where nonlinear regressions provided a better fit. All models were implemented using the chngpt99 and gam100 packages in R.

Moving-window analysis
We evaluated how the relationships between diversity and SOC in plant and soil microbial communities change along gradients of N enrichment using a moving-window approach. Linear mixed-effects models were applied to successive subsets of paired diversity–SOC observations, beginning with the lowest N enrichment values and iteratively shifting the window by one observation until the window limit was reached, with study ID included as a random factor101. Following previous studies102,103, the window size was set to 20 observations. For each subset, standardized coefficients of diversity with N rates were bootstrapped and aligned with the average N rate value of the subset101. Linear and nonlinear regressions were then used to identify N rate thresholds, with their validity tested using the methods outlined above.

Global distribution of above- and belowground biomass under N enrichment
Global data collection. Using the important predictors identified by the random forest models, we generated global spatial predictions for the responses of plant biomass, MBC, and SOC under N enrichment. In the absence of global N enrichment data, we substituted N deposition rates from Ackerman et al. for the global map values to represent N availability66. Plant diversity data were sourced from Cai et al. (https://gift.uni-goettingen.de/shiny/predictions)104. Soil biodiversity data from the project of Global Soil Biodiversity Atlas (https://esdac.jrc.ec.europa.eu/content/global-soil-biodiversity-atlas) were used as a proxy for soil microbial diversity. Climatic variables were obtained from Worldclim 2.0 (http://www.worldclim.org) based on location data. Soil properties such as pH and total N (TN) were extracted from SoilGrids (http://www.isric.org/explore/soilgrid). All covariate map layers were resampled and reprojected to a unified 0.25°-pixel grid in EPSG:4326 (WGS84). Higher-resolution layers were down-sampled using mean aggregation, while lower-resolution layers were up-sampled without interpolation to match the grid.

Prediction validation. We applied a random forest model to upscale site-level responses of plant biomass, MBC, and SOC under N enrichment to the regional scale, considering contemporary climate scenarios. Each tree in the model was trained on a randomly selected subset of data, with out-of-bag data used to estimate prediction error and variable importance105. Validation against observed data yielded Pearson’s r values of 0.54, 0.58, and 0.52 for plant biomass, MBC, and SOC, respectively (P<0.001) (Supplementary Fig. 14). The random forest training was repeated 1000 times, and the average predictions from these iterations were taken as the final variable estimates. All random forest computations were performed using the RandomForestRegressor function in the scikit-learn package in Python version 3.7106. The potential effects of global N deposition on these variables were then spatially extrapolated for each pixel using model parameters and the selected variables. Extrapolation and geospatial analyses were conducted in Python version 3.7 and ArcGIS version 10.4.1107,108. Prediction uncertainty for the global estimates was quantified as the 95% CIs (Supplementary Fig. 15).

Publication bias
To assess potential bias in our collected dataset, we employed three independent approaches. First, we utilized a funnel plot to visually examine the possibility of bias (Supplementary Fig. 16). To quantitatively test for asymmetry in the funnel plot, we applied Egger’s regression test109 (Supplementary Table 2). In cases where asymmetry was detected, we used the Rosenberg fail-safe number (Nfs) to determine the extent to which unpublished studies might influence our conclusions110. If the Nfs is larger than 5k+10 (k, number of study observations) (Supplementary Table 2), the results are robust regardless of any potential publication bias. Lastly, we evaluated the robustness of our results by performing a leave-one-out analysis using the leave1out function111 (Supplementary Fig. 17). These findings indicate that publication bias is unlikely to affect the interpretation of our results.

The authors conducted a meta-analysis to identify the threshold point of nitrogen addition that significantly reduces plant, bacterial, and fungal diversity on a global scale. They also aim to determine the critical point for soil organic carbon (SOC) accumulation under nitrogen enrichment along the nitrogen gradient. By examining the relationship between diversity and SOC responses along this gradient, the authors seek to identify critical thresholds for the co-benefits of carbon sequestration and biodiversity conservation under global nitrogen enrichment.
Several issues within the text require clarification. First, it is important to note that there may not always be a trade-off between diversity response and SOC response; at certain points, both parameters can exhibit either positive or negative responses to nitrogen enrichment. Second, the interpretation of the data presented in the main figures is challenging. In some cases, the authors find a negative correlation between plant/bacterial diversity and SOC, but this negative correlation appears to stem from the nitrogen-induced divergent responses of these parameters rather than reflecting biological significance. Although significant correlations are identified, their implications may not be fully clear.
Lastly, I believe the authors should exercise greater caution with their citations. In multiple instances, incorrect papers are cited, or the cited papers do not align with the authors’ claims. I have listed a few examples below for your check.
I have provided detailed comments below:

They also aim to determine the critical point for soil organic carbon (SOC) accumulation under nitrogen enrichment along the nitrogen gradient. We have carefully considered all the reviewer’s suggestions and have made substantial revisions accordingly. Below, we provide detailed point-by-point responses.
Comment 1: First, it is important to note that there may not always be a trade-off between diversity response and SOC response; at certain points, both parameters can exhibit either positive or negative responses to nitrogen enrichment.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. We fully agree with the reviewer that the trade-off between diversity responses and SOC responses does not always apply universally, and that both parameters can, in some cases, exhibit either positive or negative responses to nitrogen enrichment. We have rewritten paragraphs 1 and 2 of the Introduction section to better capture the variability and context-dependency in the response of diversity and SOC to N enrichment, as following: “Soil is the largest carbon (C) reservoir in terrestrial ecosystems, playing a critical role in regulating the global C cycle. Even small changes in the soil organic carbon (SOC) pool can have profound impacts on ecosystem services and land C–climate feedbacks1,2. Soil N availability significantly influences storage capacity of SOC, since N is a key component of SOC 3,4. While increased N input has alleviated constraints on global food production, it has also elevated ecosystem N availability, leading to eutrophication and altered ecosystem processes5-7. Numerous studies have demonstrated that N enrichment can enhance SOC storage by promoting the formation of larger soil aggregates, improving soil fractions, and increasing N use efficiency8-11. However, N addition does not consistently promote SOC accumulation, with some studies reporting neutral or negative effects12,13. These inconsistencies arise from the interplay of multiple drivers, such as plant and microbial biomass inputs, mineral associations, environmental conditions, and biodiversity-driven catabolism and anabolism, which collectively shape SOC formation and turnover14-17. Biodiversity is well-known in supporting SOC accumulation18,19, thus its responses to N enrichment could profoundly reshape SOC dynamics. N enrichment has been shown to reduce biodiversity of both above- and belowground communities20,21, primarily through mechanisms such as competitive exclusion, soil acidification and cation toxicity22-24. However, some studies have reported that N addition exerts only minor effects on soil microbial diversity, particularly within fungal communities25. These shifts can disrupt the balance between C and nutrient demands in plants and soil microbes, potentially decoupling their interactions or generating context-dependent responses that alter ecosystem C fluxes between above- and belowground compartments, ultimately affecting SOC dynamics14,18,26-30. Despite increasing evidence of such complexities9,11,31,32, few studies have simultaneously evaluated the relative contributions of fundamental drivers to SOC response under N enrichment, particularly regarding whether and how biodiversity mediates SOC dynamics. Therefore, a global assessment of the factors underpinning SOC dynamics is critical for reducing the uncertainty in biogeochemical models of soil C turnover and advancing our understanding of how biodiversity supports soil carbon stocks in an N-enriched world33.
Biodiversity and carbon conservation are dual priorities in the global effort to mitigate climate change34. However, the divergent responses of biodiversity and SOC under N enrichment pose a challenge to achieving both goals simultaneously, as their co-occurrence may ultimately undermine long-term synergies30. This tension underscores the need to identify critical thresholds along N enrichment gradients, beyond which biodiversity losses may accelerate even as carbon stocks continue to rise35,36. Recognizing and quantifying these ecological thresholds is increasingly pivotal for ecosystem-based management and policy formulation, as they offer valuable benchmarks for designing effective management interventions and conservation targets37-40. Although previous studies have documented nonlinear or saturating responses of biodiversity and SOC to N enrichment, critical thresholds along N gradients have yet to be systematically quantified. Given their higher sensitivity to environmental change41, soil microbial communities are likely to exhibit detectable threshold responses earlier than plants along N gradients. Such shifts in microbial and plant communities may modify soil properties in ways that delay the manifestation of SOC thresholds relative to biodiversity thresholds. Understanding how biodiversity and SOC in terrestrial ecosystems respond to increasing N inputs is critical for advancing ecological threshold theory and informing estimates of N input levels that agroecosystems and natural ecosystems can tolerate before facing heightened risks of biodiversity loss, carbon destabilization, and eutrophication.”. (Line 34-76)
Comment 2: Second, the interpretation of the data presented in the main figures is challenging. In some cases, the authors find a negative correlation between plant/bacterial diversity and SOC, but this negative correlation appears to stem from the nitrogen-induced divergent responses of these parameters rather than reflecting biological significance. Response: We fully thank the reviewer this valuable comments. We recognize that the original version lacked sufficient clarity in describing and discussing the results (as raised in Comment 6) and their ecological significance (as raised in Comment 27). To improve the interpretation of the origin Fig. 3, we have enhanced this section in two ways: (1) providing a clear interpretive framework to guide readers in understanding the ecological meaning of the point distributions and fitted trends, and (2) revising the Results and Discussion sections to offer a more detailed and structured interpretation of the observed patterns. The details are provided below:
1. Interpretive framework. We first clarify the interpretive framework for understanding Fig. 3b-d. Each dot in the moving-window analysis represents the correlation between biodiversity (lnRR) and SOC (lnRR) sliding N addition window. A complete ecological interpretation of these correlations requires consideration of two dimensions: (1) The sign of the correlation coefficient (relative to the zero line, where correlation > 0 indicates a positive relationship and < 0 indicates a negative one), indicating whether biodiversity and SOC change in the same direction (i.e., co-increase or co-decline, positive correlation), or in opposite directions (negative correlation); (2) The trend of correlation strength across the nitrogen gradient, where a positive slope indicates strengthening biodiversity-SOC coupling with increasing N, while a negative slope suggests weakening or decoupling. Additionally, the final ecological interpretation integrates not only the overall effect sizes but also their directional shifts across the N enrichment threshold, providing a more comprehensive understanding of biodiversity and SOC dynamics. Based on this framework, we reorganized the text to more clearly delineate zones of biodiversity-SOC synergy and decoupling along the nitrogen gradient. This framework was used to reorganize the text and better delineate zones of biodiversity-SOC synergy or decoupling along the N gradient.
2. Detailed results and interpretation. In Fig. 3b, bacterial diversity and SOC showed a slightly negative correlation below ~50 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹, reflecting a decoupled pattern where bacterial diversity declined slightly while SOC continued to increase under low-N inputs. As N input exceeded this threshold, the correlation gradually shifted toward positive (reaching ~200 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹), suggesting the onset of a co-decline phase where intensified N enrichment simultaneously undermines both biodiversity and carbon accumulation. In Fig. 3c, the response of fungal diversity fluctuated around ~67 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ but maintained a generally positive correlation with SOC across the gradient, likely because its weak negative response to N enrichment did not disrupt its sustained functional role in carbon stabilization (e.g., via aggregate formation). In Fig. 3d, the plant diversity–SOC relationship followed a stronger nonlinear pattern. At low N inputs (<50 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹), we observed strong negative correlations, reflecting a decoupled pattern where diversity loss driven by light competition and cation toxicity occurred alongside continued SOC accumulation. Between 50–74 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹, the correlation became strongly positive, indicating a phase where accelerating biodiversity decline was accompanied by weakening or even reversing SOC accumulation, marking the onset of co-decline dynamics. However, beyond ~74 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹, although the correlation between plant diversity and SOC responses remained positive, the slope turned negative, signaling a weakening biodiversity–SOC coupling. This likely reflects that severe species loss and functional homogenization increasingly uncouple plant diversity from SOC dynamics, potentially undermining future soil carbon gains. These findings consistently demonstrate a trajectory of low-N decoupling, mid-N synergy, and high-N functional breakdown across microbial and plant communities, marking a shift from indirect N-driven SOC gains, to biodiversity-mediated regulation, and ultimately to diversity-imposed constraints under N saturation. Overall, this gradient-dependent transition from synergy to trade-off highlights the complex and multifaceted impacts of biodiversity loss on SOC storage capacity.

3. Our classification, urea (CO(NH₂)₂) was treated as a separate category (“Urea N”) rather than being grouped under “Organic N”. Although urea is chemically an organic compound, its biogeochemical behavior in soils aligns more closely with inorganic nitrogen sources due to its rapid hydrolysis into ammonium (NH₄⁺) in soils, bypassing the slow mineralization of traditional organic amendments (e.g., compost, manure). This dynamic behavior necessitates its separate classification as "Urea N" to avoid conflating it with stable organic nitrogen pools. Therefore, given the ecological relevance and consistency with previous research (ref. 1-2), we categorized urea separately to better capture its unique dynamics in the nitrogen cycle. We have revised the manuscript to clarify this rationale in Line 705-707.
4. “Organic N” refers specifically to nitrogen inputs derived from organic sources, including industrial organic fertilizers, livestock manure, and compost. We have added this definition in the legend of Fig. 1: “Organic N refers to industrial organic fertilizers, livestock manure, and compost.”.
5. We have revised the x-axis label from “Mean effect size of N enrichment (%)” to “Mean effect size (%) of N enrichment” in the revised Fig. 1.

Comment 6: Fig. 3: The results are difficult to interpret. In panel b, if we examine the absolute values for most cases, most relationships fall below the zero line, suggesting that higher bacterial diversity leads to lower SOC. If this is the case, why should we prioritize the protection of bacterial diversity? Similarly, in panel d, if I understand correctly, most relationships are negative below 40 kg N, indicating that a higher response in plant diversity corresponds to a lower response in SOC. In such cases, why is it important to protect plant diversity?
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this valuable comment. In Fig. 3b and 3d, each data point represents the correlation between the lnRR of diversity and that of SOC within a sliding N addition window. This approach captures shifts in co-response patterns along the nitrogen gradient, rather than indicating static or one-directional causal relationships.
To address the concern regarding the difficulty of interpreting Fig. 3b-d, we have enhanced this section in two ways: (1) by providing a clear interpretive framework to guide readers in understanding the ecological meaning of the point distributions and fitted trends, and (2) by revising the Results and Discussion sections to offer a more detailed and structured interpretation of the observed patterns. The details are provided below:
1. We first clarify the interpretive framework for understanding Fig. 3b-d. Each dot in the moving-window analysis represents the correlation between biodiversity (lnRR) and SOC (lnRR) sliding N addition window. A complete ecological interpretation of these correlations requires consideration of two dimensions: (1) The sign of the correlation coefficient (relative to the zero line, where correlation > 0 indicates a positive relationship and < 0 indicates a negative one), indicating whether biodiversity and SOC change in the same direction (i.e., co-increase or co-decline, positive correlation), or in opposite directions (negative correlation); (2) The trend of correlation strength across the nitrogen gradient, where a positive slope indicates strengthening biodiversity-SOC coupling with increasing N, while a negative slope suggests weakening or decoupling. Additionally, the final ecological interpretation integrates not only the overall effect sizes but also their directional shifts across the N enrichment threshold, providing a more comprehensive understanding of biodiversity and SOC dynamics. Based on this framework, we reorganized the text to more clearly delineate zones of biodiversity-SOC synergy and decoupling along the nitrogen gradient. This framework was used to reorganize the text and better delineate zones of biodiversity-SOC synergy or decoupling along the N gradient.
We have also included a concise explanation in the legend of Fig. 3 to enhance the readability and aid interpretation as: “Moving-window correlations between the response of diversity and the response of SOC along N gradients for bacteria (b), fungi (c), and plants (d). The dots indicate the bootstrapped coefficients of the fixed terms shown for each subset window. The sign of each dot (relative to the zero line, where values > 0 indicate positive associations and values < 0 indicate negative associations) reflects whether biodiversity and SOC respond in the same (co-increase or co-decline) or in opposite directions. The slope of the fitted line indicates how biodiversity-SOC associations change across the N gradient: a positive slope suggests strengthening associations with increasing N input, whereas a negative slope suggests weakening or reversal.”. (Line 731-739)
2. In Fig. 3b, bacterial diversity and SOC showed a slightly negative correlation below ~50 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹, reflecting a decoupled pattern where bacterial diversity declined slightly while SOC continued to increase under low-N inputs. As N input exceeded this threshold, the correlation gradually shifted toward positive (reaching ~200 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹), suggesting the onset of a co-decline phase where intensified N enrichment simultaneously undermines both biodiversity and carbon accumulation. In Fig. 3c, the response of fungal diversity fluctuated around ~67 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ but maintained a generally positive correlation with SOC across the gradient, likely because its weak negative response to N enrichment did not disrupt its sustained functional role in carbon stabilization (e.g., via aggregate formation). In Fig. 3d, the plant diversity–SOC relationship followed a stronger nonlinear pattern. At low N inputs (<50 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹), we observed strong negative correlations, reflecting a decoupled pattern where diversity loss driven by light competition and cation toxicity occurred alongside continued SOC accumulation. Between 50–74 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹, the correlation became strongly positive, indicating a phase where accelerating biodiversity decline was accompanied by weakening or even reversing SOC accumulation, marking the onset of co-decline dynamics. However, beyond ~74 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹, although the correlation between plant diversity and SOC responses remained positive, the slope turned negative, signaling a weakening biodiversity–SOC coupling. This likely reflects that severe species loss and functional homogenization increasingly uncouple plant diversity from SOC dynamics, potentially undermining future soil carbon gains. These findings consistently demonstrate a trajectory of low-N decoupling, mid-N synergy, and high-N functional breakdown across microbial and plant communities, marking a shift from indirect N-driven SOC gains, to biodiversity-mediated regulation, and ultimately to diversity-imposed constraints under N saturation. Overall, this gradient-dependent transition from synergy to trade-off highlights the complex and multifaceted impacts of biodiversity loss on SOC storage capacity.
We have re-written this paragraph and updated this clearly version in Results and Discussion in the revision as: “Moreover, we performed a moving-window analysis to evaluate the potential shifts in the relationships between diversity and SOC with increasing N (Fig. 4b-d and Fig. S8). The correlation between bacterial diversity and SOC initially exhibited a short-term negative relationship below the threshold, while fungal diversity maintained a positive correlation both before and after the threshold, though the strength of the positive correlation weakened beyond it. In contrast, the relationship between plant diversity and SOC shifted dramatically, transitioning from a positive to a negative correlation once the threshold was exceeded. The responses of bacterial diversity and SOC showed a slightly negative correlation below ~50 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ (Fig. 4b), reflecting a decoupled pattern where bacterial diversity declined slightly while SOC continued to increase under low-N inputs. As N input exceeded this threshold, the correlation gradually shifted toward positive (reaching ~200 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹), suggesting the onset of a co-decline phase where intensified N enrichment simultaneously undermines both biodiversity and carbon accumulation. The response of fungal diversity fluctuated around ~67 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ but maintained a generally positive correlation with SOC across the N gradient (Fig. 4c), likely because its weak negative response to N enrichment did not disrupt its sustained functional role in carbon stabilization70. At low N inputs (<50 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹), strong negative correlations emerged between the responses of plant diversity and SOC (Fig. 4d), reflecting a decoupled pattern where diversity loss driven by light competition and cation toxicity occurred alongside continued SOC accumulation22. Between 50-74 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹, the correlation became strongly positive, indicating a phase where accelerating biodiversity decline was accompanied by weakening or even reversing SOC accumulation, marking the onset of co-decline dynamics. However, beyond ~74 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹, although the correlation between plant diversity and SOC responses remained positive, the slope of this relationship turned negative, signaling a weakening biodiversity-SOC coupling. This pattern likely reflects that severe species loss and functional homogenization increasingly uncouple plant diversity from SOC dynamics, potentially undermining future soil carbon gains30. These findings consistently reveal a trajectory of low-N decoupling, mid-N synergy, and high-N functional breakdown across microbial and plant communities, marking a shift from indirect N-driven SOC gains, to biodiversity-mediated regulation, and ultimately to diversity-imposed constraints under N saturation. Overall, this gradient-dependent transition from synergy to trade-off underscores the complex and multifaceted consequences of biodiversity loss for SOC accumulation. Limiting N inputs to below 50 kg N ha⁻¹·yr⁻¹ could help mitigate biodiversity loss and its negative effects on SOC storage, supporting long-term ecosystem stability.”. (Line 244-275)
Comment 7: Fig 4: Fig 4 seems out of the logic flow of the main story. All other figs target on the diversity effect on SOC, why Figure 4 focus on biomass and SOC?
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We would like to clarify that the global distributions presented in Fig. 4 were not intended to investigate the causal effects of biomass on SOC. Instead, the distributions of plant biomass, microbial biomass (MBC), and SOC were modeled independently, after accounting for climatic factors, soil properties, and diversity effects, to provide parallel and comprehensive insights into ecosystem carbon dynamics under N enrichment. Given that plant and microbial biomass constitute the immediate material basis for SOC formation and turnover, we believe presenting these distributions may help provide broader context for the observed SOC responses and illustrate the decoupled and complex above- and belowground processes under N enrichment. Importantly, we recognize that the ecological pathways linking biodiversity, biomass, and SOC differ between microbial and plant communities: in microbial communities, changes in biodiversity can directly influence microbial biomass and stabilization processes, whereas in plant communities, N-induced biomass accumulation may precede and contribute to biodiversity loss, with both processes jointly modifying soil carbon inputs and stabilization pathways.
Therefore, we have retained Fig. 4 and repositioned it earlier in the manuscript (now Fig. 2), following the random forest analysis (origin Fig. 2) and before the diversity-SOC coupling section, to better align with the main narrative. This repositioning, together with the clarification that biomass and SOC projections were modeled independently, aims to strengthen the logical flow and avoid potential misinterpretations about causal pathways. Here, we would briefly highlight that Fig. 4 presents global-scale distributions of plant and microbial biomass, as well as SOC responses under N enrichment. Panel a shows widespread increases in plant biomass across most regions, consistent with nitrogen-stimulated productivity. Panel b reveals a more heterogeneous pattern for microbial biomass (MBC): while low-latitude (tropical) and high-latitude (boreal/polar) regions generally show positive responses, strong negative responses are evident in many mid-latitude areas, particularly in temperate ecosystems such as central North America, Europe, and parts of East Asia. This spatial asymmetry likely reflects regional differences in baseline nutrient availability, microbial community sensitivity, and climatic constraints on microbial turnover. Panel c indicates that SOC generally exhibits positive responses across much of the temperate Northern Hemisphere, particularly in regions such as Europe and central to northern Asia, where both plant carbon inputs and microbial transformation potential may be relatively high. In contrast, negative responses are more prevalent in many parts of the Southern Hemisphere and tropical zones, including southern Africa and parts of South and Southeast Asia. These patterns may reflect combined limitations such as reduced microbial activity or accelerated carbon mineralization under warmer and more nutrient-enriched conditions. Together, these spatial patterns provide complementary insights into the complex ways in which nitrogen enrichment reshapes ecosystem carbon dynamics across different climatic regions.
To further improve the logical flow, we have then added an introductory sentence at the beginning of the paragraph to better clarify how the global biomass projections relate to biodiversity-mediated regulation of SOC dynamics. In addition, we have substantially shortened this section and no longer present these global distributions as a standalone subsection. In addition, the figure is now briefly incorporated into a broader discussion of N-mediated ecosystem-level shifts, serving as a further extension of the the global patterns of N enrichment effects on biodiversity and ecosystem carbon stocks. The revised paragraph now reads as follows: “Given that plant and microbial biomass constitute the immediate foundation for SOC formation and turnover, we independently modelled the global responses of plant biomass, microbial biomass, and SOC under N enrichment to better elucidate ecosystem carbon dynamics (Fig. 2). Positive plant biomass responses largely dominated across the globe, particularly in temperate and boreal regions of North America, Europe, and Asia, reflecting N-stimulated productivity60 (Fig. 2a). In contrast, microbial biomass (MBC) exhibited greater regional heterogeneity, with positive responses concentrated in tropical and boreal zones but widespread declines across mid-latitude temperate ecosystems, including central North America, Europe, and East Asia (Fig. 2b). This spatial divergence likely reflects regional differences in background N deposition and soil sensitivity: in tropical and boreal zones with low ambient N, moderate enrichment promotes microbial growth, whereas in temperate regions with higher baseline N inputs, further enrichment induces acidification and nutrient imbalance, suppressing biomass61,62. Similarly, SOC responses were largely positive across temperate regions, particularly in Europe and northern Asia, whereas negative responses prevailed in parts of the Southern Hemisphere and tropical zones, including southern Africa, South Asia, and Southeast Asia (Fig. 2c). This likely reflects differences in nutrient limitations and ecosystem processes: in temperate systems, nitrogen (N) addition tends to stimulate plant growth and inputs while simultaneously reducing decomposition rates, thereby promoting SOC accumulation; in tropical and Southern Hemisphere regions, where phosphorus limitation and rapid organic matter turnover are more common, N addition often fails to enhance plant inputs and may even accelerate SOC loss63,64. Together, these spatial patterns illustrate how N enrichment reshapes carbon cycling across climatic gradients and emphasize the importance of region-specific N management aligned with carbon accumulation objectives.”. (Line 155-176)
Nonetheless, if the revised presentation still does not fully resolve the concern, we are happy to remove the origin Fig. 4 along with the associated text in the final version, and we also remain fully open to any further suggestions from the reviewer.

Comment 10: Lines 35-42: These statements suggest that there must be a trade-off between SOC accumulation and biodiversity loss under nitrogen addition; however, this may not be accurate. What if, at certain points, both SOC and biodiversity increase with nitrogen addition? In such cases, no trade-offs would exist.
Response: We fully agree with the reviewer that a trade-off between SOC accumulation and biodiversity loss is not a universal outcome under N enrichment. For example, bacterial richness has been shown to increase under low levels of nitrogen input (ref. 1), and SOC accumulation was also observed under similar conditions (ref. 2). In such cases, biodiversity and SOC may respond in parallel, suggesting a coupled or synergistic relationship rather than a trade-off. We acknowledge that the original tone could be interpreted as overly categorical, and we have revised the text accordingly to better reflect the variability and context-dependency of biodiversity-SOC relationships under N enrichment.
The revised sentences of paragraph 1 in Introduction as: “While increased N input has alleviated constraints on global food production, it has also elevated ecosystem N availability, leading to eutrophication and altered ecosystem processes5-7. Numerous studies have demonstrated that N enrichment can enhance SOC storage by promoting the formation of larger soil aggregates, improving soil fractions, and increasing N use efficiency8-11. However, N addition does not consistently promote SOC accumulation, with some studies reporting neutral or negative effects12,13. These inconsistencies arise from the interplay of multiple drivers, such as plant and microbial biomass inputs, mineral associations, environmental conditions, and biodiversity-driven catabolism and anabolism, which collectively shape SOC formation and turnover14-17. Biodiversity is well-known in supporting SOC accumulation18,19, thus its responses to N enrichment could profoundly reshape SOC dynamics. N enrichment has been shown to reduce biodiversity of both above- and belowground communities20,21, primarily through mechanisms such as competitive exclusion, soil acidification and cation toxicity22-24. However, some studies have reported that N addition exerts only minor effects on soil microbial diversity, particularly within fungal communities25. These shifts can disrupt the balance between C and nutrient demands in plants and soil microbes, potentially decoupling their interactions or generating context-dependent responses that alter ecosystem C fluxes between above- and belowground compartments, ultimately affecting SOC dynamics14,18,26-30.”. (Line 37-54)
Additionally, we have also revised the first sentence of paragraph 2 in Introduction “The trade-off between biodiversity loss and SOC accumulation highlights the necessity of balanced N management strategies” to a more moderate tone. The revised sentence as: “Biodiversity and carbon conservation are dual priorities in the global effort to mitigate climate change34. However, the divergent responses of biodiversity and SOC under N enrichment pose a challenge to achieving both goals simultaneously, as their co-occurrence may ultimately undermine long-term synergies30.” (Line 60-63)

Response: We have carefully revised the Introduction section as suggested, and greatly appreciate the reviewer’s insightful feedback, which inspired us to more clearly highlight how nitrogen thresholds may influence the coupling or decoupling between biodiversity and soil carbon dynamics, thus raising an important perspective that was not sufficiently emphasized in the original version. Moreover, we believe that the conceptual framework refined through this revision may offer broader insights for identifying ecological thresholds under other global change drivers, particularly when synthesizing complex biodiversity and ecosystem function responses through large-scale meta-analyses. Specifically, we addressed the following four aspects, organized according to the logical flow of the Introduction:
1. We added more detailed background information on the differential responses of plant and soil microbial communities to N enrichment, acknowledging that some microbial groups exhibit minor or inconsistent diversity changes.
2. We clarified the rationale for threshold analyses and more explicitly discussed ecological expectations regarding which thresholds (plant vs. microbial) might be reached earlier and why.
3. We revised the description of SOC responses to nitrogen enrichment to include not only positive but also neutral and negative outcomes reported in previous studies.
4. We emphasized that SOC dynamics are shaped by the interplay of multiple factors, including plant and microbial biomass inputs, catabolic and anabolic processes, soil physicochemical properties, and biodiversity shifts.
The revised first and second paragraph of Introduction as: “Soil is the largest carbon (C) reservoir in terrestrial ecosystems, playing a critical role in regulating the global C cycle. Even small changes in the soil organic carbon (SOC) pool can have profound impacts on ecosystem services and land C–climate feedbacks1,2. Soil N availability significantly influences storage capacity of SOC, since N is a key component of SOC 3,4. While increased N input has alleviated constraints on global food production, it has also elevated ecosystem N availability, leading to eutrophication and altered ecosystem processes5-7. Numerous studies have demonstrated that N enrichment can enhance SOC storage by promoting the formation of larger soil aggregates, improving soil fractions, and increasing N use efficiency8-11. However, N addition does not consistently promote SOC accumulation, with some studies reporting neutral or negative effects12,13. These inconsistencies arise from the interplay of multiple drivers, such as plant and microbial biomass inputs, mineral associations, environmental conditions, and biodiversity-driven catabolism and anabolism, which collectively shape SOC formation and turnover14-17. Biodiversity is well-known in supporting SOC accumulation18,19, thus its responses to N enrichment could profoundly reshape SOC dynamics. N enrichment has been shown to reduce biodiversity of both above- and belowground communities20,21, primarily through mechanisms such as competitive exclusion, soil acidification and cation toxicity22-24. However, some studies have reported that N addition exerts only minor effects on soil microbial diversity, particularly within fungal communities25. These shifts can disrupt the balance between C and nutrient demands in plants and soil microbes, potentially decoupling their interactions or generating context-dependent responses that alter ecosystem C fluxes between above- and belowground compartments, ultimately affecting SOC dynamics14,18,26-30. Despite increasing evidence of such complexities9,11,31,32, few studies have simultaneously evaluated the relative contributions of fundamental drivers to SOC response under N enrichment, particularly regarding whether and how biodiversity mediates SOC dynamics. Therefore, a global assessment of the factors underpinning SOC dynamics is critical for reducing the uncertainty in biogeochemical models of soil C turnover and advancing our understanding of how biodiversity supports soil carbon stocks in an N-enriched world33.
Biodiversity and carbon conservation are dual priorities in the global effort to mitigate climate change34. However, the divergent responses of biodiversity and SOC under N enrichment pose a challenge to achieving both goals simultaneously, as their co-occurrence may ultimately undermine long-term synergies30. This tension underscores the need to identify critical thresholds along N enrichment gradients, beyond which biodiversity losses may accelerate even as carbon stocks continue to rise35,36. Recognizing and quantifying these ecological thresholds is increasingly pivotal for ecosystem-based management and policy formulation, as they offer valuable benchmarks for designing effective management interventions and conservation targets37-40. Although previous studies have documented nonlinear or saturating responses of biodiversity and SOC to N enrichment, critical thresholds along N gradients have yet to be systematically quantified. Given their higher sensitivity to environmental change41, soil microbial communities are likely to exhibit detectable threshold responses earlier than plants along N gradients. Such shifts in microbial and plant communities may modify soil properties in ways that delay the manifestation of SOC thresholds relative to biodiversity thresholds. Understanding how biodiversity and SOC in terrestrial ecosystems respond to increasing N inputs is critical for advancing ecological threshold theory and informing estimates of N input levels that agroecosystems and natural ecosystems can tolerate before facing heightened risks of biodiversity loss, carbon destabilization, and eutrophication.”. (Line 34-76)

Comment 24: Line 146: Is plant diversity the most important factor? How does the model account for the collinearity of plant diversity and SOC along the nitrogen addition gradient? Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising these important points. Firstly, we acknowledge that in the original wording, our aim is to highlight the important role of plant diversity in driving SOC responses under nitrogen enrichment by stating “except for TN”. However, we realize that this phrasing may have led to confusion during quick reading, potentially obscuring the actual ranking of predictor importance. Second, we would like to clarify that potential collinearity between plant diversity and SOC was already carefully considered during our original analysis. Specifically, prior to model fitting, we applied a two-step variable selection procedure using the spatialRF package (Benito et al., 2021) followed by Sáez-Sandino et.al (Nat. Clim. Chang., 2023): (1) correlation-based filtering (auto_cor function, r > 0.6) to remove highly correlated predictors, and (2) variance inflation factor filtering (auto_vif function, VIF > 2.5) to further exclude N-induced collinear variables. This procedure ensured that only predictors with low intercorrelations and acceptable multicollinearity levels were retained for model construction, thereby preserving the ecological interpretability of our Random Forest results. Additionally, predictor importance was assessed by measuring the mean decrease in prediction accuracy (mean squared error) when each predictor was permuted across trees, and model performance was evaluated using out-of-bag error estimates, providing an internal, unbiased measure of predictive accuracy. We have now added this methodological detail more explicitly in the revised Methods section as: “…Before model fitting, we minimized multicollinearity by performing two steps: (1) correlation-based filtering (auto_cor function, r > 0.6) to remove highly correlated predictors, and (2) variance inflation factor filtering (auto_vif function, VIF > 2.5) to further exclude N-induced collinear variables…”. (Line 392-395)
Third, we agree that the results from the Random Forest analysis and the meta-regression presented in panel f may initially appear different; however, they reflect different analytical perspectives rather than a contradiction. Specifically, the Random Forest analysis evaluated the relative contribution of multiple predictors to SOC responses across N enrichment gradients, identifying plant diversity response as a stronger predictor compared to microbial diversity in a multivariate modeling context. This reflects how plant diversity changes, alongside other variables, jointly contribute to SOC variation when interactions among predictors are considered. In contrast, the meta-regression analysis in panel f examined the pairwise correlation between diversity responses and SOC responses individually, without controlling for other variables. In this framework, microbial diversity (particularly fungal diversity) showed a slightly stronger direct association with SOC change than plant diversity. Thus, the two analyses offer complementary insights: Random Forest identifies the key predictors influencing SOC when multiple factors interact; Meta-regression captures the strength of individual diversity-SOC relationships. We believe that together, these approaches provide a more comprehensive understanding of the pathways through which biodiversity changes influence SOC dynamics under N enrichment.

Comment 27: Lines 196-220: You discuss only the strength of correlations, but the direction and underlying biological significance are also crucial for interpretation. I am unclear about what the authors or the figures are attempting to convey.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for highlighting the need to clarify not only the strength but also the direction and biological significance of the observed correlations. In the revised manuscript, we now explicitly detail how the relationships between biodiversity (bacterial, fungal, and plant) and SOC shift across the N gradient, capturing both the correlation direction and the underlying ecological dynamics. Our findings consistently reveal a clear trajectory: a phase of low-N decoupling where biodiversity and SOC respond independently, followed by mid-N synergy where diversity loss begins constraining SOC accumulation, and ultimately high-N functional breakdown, where intensified N saturation simultaneously undermines biodiversity and carbon storage. This gradient-dependent transition from synergy to trade-off highlights the urgent need to recognize biodiversity as a critical regulator of carbon cycling under global N enrichment. We conclude that limiting N inputs to below ~50 kg N ha⁻¹·yr⁻¹ may help safeguard both biodiversity and long-term soil carbon storage, offering crucial benchmarks for ecosystem management and policy.

I have reviewed the revised manuscript titled "Critical Thresholds for Co-Benefits of Carbon Sequestration and Biodiversity Conservation Under Global Nitrogen Enrichment (NC-574816)." Your earlier feedback was instrumental in helping us substantially improve the manuscript, particularly in terms of logical structure, the meta-regression analyses, textual clarity, discussion, and figure presentation. We provide detailed, point-by-point responses below and look forward to your further comments.
Comment 1 (Line 45): The term “biodiversity-driven catabolism and anabolism” is unclear. Please provide a definition or explanation of these concepts and how they relate to the study's objectives.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. The previously used term “biodiversity-driven catabolism and anabolism” refers to microbial diversity-mediated processes of organic matter decomposition (catabolism) and microbial biomass and extracellular product formation (anabolism). These processes are jointly regulated by microbial carbon use efficiency (CUE), which is shaped by microbial diversity. In parallel, plant diversity contributes to C cycling by diversifying organic inputs (e.g., litter and root exudates), while microbial diversity determines how efficiently these inputs are processed and transformed. Together, these mechanisms align with theories of functional trait diversity and niche complementarity, thereby supporting our study’s objective of elucidating how biodiversity regulates SOC dynamics under N enrichment. We have revised these descriptions to elaborate on the mechanisms through which plant and soil microbial diversity influence soil carbon (C) dynamics to better link biodiversity with SOC outcomes, as: “The inconsistencies may arise from differences in substrate quantity, mineral associations, environmental conditions and biodiversity13. Biodiversity, in particular, is widely recognized to regulate soil C cycling14,15, with its loss driving large-scale changes in ecosystem energy flow and nutrient cycling16,17. Higher plant diversity often increases biomass inputs and root exudation18, while soil microbial diversity governs the balance between C catabolism (decomposition) and anabolism (biomass and extracellular production)19-21, thereby shaping SOC dynamics.”. (Line 40-46)
Comment 2 (Lines 49-51): The logical flow is confusing. You state that nitrogen (N) addition reduces plant diversity but not microbial diversity. Subsequently, you claim that these shifts can disrupt the balance. What specific shifts are you referring to, and how do they disrupt the ecological balance? Please clarify.
Response: We thank the reviewer for highlighting this point and for the opportunity to clarify the logical flow in our original text. Our intention was to emphasize the complex and often divergent responses of plant and soil microbial diversity to N enrichment, and how such differential responses may influence SOC dynamics. It is well established that N enrichment typically reduces plant diversity, primarily through mechanisms such as competitive exclusion, light limitation due to increased canopy dominance, and changes in soil chemistry. In contrast, microbial responses to N addition are more variable and taxon-dependent. For instance, Wang et al. (2023, Soil Biology and Biochemistry) reported that while N enrichment significantly reduced overall microbial alpha diversity, this effect was primarily driven by declines in bacterial diversity, whereas fungal diversity did not show a statistically significant change. Importantly, other studies have similarly noted inconsistent or weak responses of fungal richness to N addition, underscoring the complex and taxon-specific nature of microbial responses to N enrichment. Such divergent responses between plant and microbial diversity may weaken the positive biodiversity effects on SOC sequestration. Moreover, the potential erosion of functional diversity could further decrease resource-use efficiency and ecosystem productivity, posing a major challenge for sustaining SOC accumulation while mitigating biodiversity loss.
We have made revision as following: “N enrichment generally reduces biodiversity22-25, primarily through mechanisms such as competitive exclusion, soil acidification and cation toxicity24,26. Yet microbial diversity exhibits inconsistent responses27,28. For example, while N enrichment significantly reduced overall microbial diversity, the decline was mainly observed for bacteria, whereas fungal diversity remained unchanged27. This highlights the complex and taxon-specific nature of microbial responses to N enrichment. Therefore, such divergent responses between plant and microbial diversity may weaken the positive biodiversity effects on SOC sequestration29,30. Moreover, the potential erosion of functional diversity could further decrease resource-use efficiency and ecosystem productivity, posing a major challenge for sustaining SOC accumulation while mitigating biodiversity loss14,19,22,31-33.” (Line 46-55)
Comment 3 (Line 55): The phrase “fundamental drivers” is vague. What specific factors are being referred to here? It is crucial in scientific writing to be precise and clear.
Response: We fully agree with the reviewer that “fundamental drivers” should be defined more explicitly. In our study, these drivers refer to key biotic, abiotic, and climatic factors that potentially regulate SOC dynamics under N enrichment. Specifically, they include above- and belowground biodiversity and biomass, soil physicochemical properties (e.g., pH, soil moisture and nutrients availability), and climatic variables (e.g., mean annual precipitation, mean annual temperature).
We have revised the sentence to clarify these components in the introduction as: “Despite increasing evidence of these complexities4,9,27,34, few studies have jointly assessed the relative contributions of major drivers, including plant and microbial diversity and biomass, soil physicochemical attributes (e.g., pH, moisture, nutrient availability), and climatic variables (e.g., mean annual precipitation, mean annual temperature), to SOC responses under N enrichment.”. (Line 55-59)
Comment 4 (Second Paragraph): The manuscript suggests a potential trade-off between diversity response and SOC response to N addition. However, this relationship is context-dependent and should not be presented as universally applicable. The writing needs further refinement to reflect this nuance.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. We fully agree that the potential trade-off between biodiversity and soil organic carbon (SOC) responses to nitrogen (N) enrichment is context-dependent and should not be generalized across all ecosystems or N input scenarios. Our original intent in the second paragraph of the Introduction was to highlight that such decoupling has been observed under specific conditions, rather than to imply a universal or inevitable pattern. We acknowledge that the initial wording lacked sufficient nuance and contextual qualifiers, such as ecosystem type, rate and duration of N addition, climate, and soil properties, that are critical in determining whether a trade-off emerges. To address this concern, we have revised the text to more explicitly frame the biodiversity-SOC relationship as conditionally mediated by ecological and experimental context. Moreover, we elaborated through three case studies to demonstrate that such trade-offs arise only under particular ecological contexts, in order to reduce the misconception that trade-offs are inevitable or universal.
The revised sentences in second paragraph as: “Biodiversity and soil C conservation are dual priorities in the global effort to mitigate climate change36,37. However, N enrichment can disrupt this synergy over time, decoupling biodiversity and C goals22. For example, a 27-year field experiment in temperate grassland reported SOC gains under high N input, but at the cost of substantial plant diversity loss38. Similarly, a global meta-analysis revealed that soil bacterial and fungal diversity are strongly negatively associated with soil C content, and their linkages are influenced by N fertilization rate and duration22. In contrast, tree species mixtures with high diversity can enhance SOC accumulation under elevated N availability39. These findings suggest that biodiversity-SOC relationships under N enrichment are context-dependent, and continued N inputs may trigger trade-offs under specific environmental conditions. Therefore, identifying ecological thresholds along N gradients is essential to anticipate when biodiversity losses may begin to undermine soil C gains40,41.”. (Line 63-73)
Comment 5: The statement that “soil microbial communities are likely to exhibit detectable threshold responses earlier than plants along N gradients” conflicts with your earlier assertion that plant diversity typically responds negatively to N addition, while microbial communities, particularly fungal diversity, show no response. Please resolve this inconsistency.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important and insightful concern. We acknowledge that the original wording may have created an apparent inconsistency between two key points: (1) that plant diversity generally shows stronger and more consistent declines in response to N enrichment, and (2) that microbial communities may exhibit threshold responses earlier along N gradients. We agree that these statements require careful contextualization to avoid misinterpretation. While plant communities often show greater magnitude of diversity loss under N enrichment, particularly in terms of species richness and evenness, microbial communities may respond differently in terms of timing and sensitivity. Despite relatively stable alpha diversity (especially in fungi), soil microbes can undergo rapid and detectable shifts in community composition, functional gene expression, or metabolic activity in response to even low levels of N addition. This high sensitivity is attributed to their short generation times, high metabolic rates, and strong coupling to soil resource chemistry. For example, studies have shown that microbial community composition (e.g., shifts in dominant taxa or functional groups) can change abruptly at relatively low N inputs, before significant changes in plant diversity are observed. These early microbial shifts may serve as leading indicators of ecosystem change, even when overall microbial richness remains unchanged. Thus, while plants may exhibit larger net losses in diversity over time, microbes may reach critical threshold responses earlier along the N gradient due to their physiological and ecological traits.
To resolve this ambiguity, we have now revised the relevant sentences as in Line 77-79: “Given their high metabolic rates and short generation times46, soil microbial communities are more sensitive and responsive to environmental changes than plants47,48”, and in Line 48-50: “Yet microbial diversity exhibits inconsistent responses27,28. For example, while N enrichment significantly reduced overall microbial diversity, the decline was mainly observed for bacteria, whereas fungal diversity remained unchanged27. This highlights the complex and taxon-specific nature of microbial responses to N enrichment.”
Comment 6: The claim that “shifts in microbial and plant communities may modify soil properties in ways that delay the manifestation of SOC thresholds relative to biodiversity thresholds” requires further explanation. Why do these shifts delay the SOC threshold? Please clarify the underlying mechanisms.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful question. We agree that our original statement regarding the delayed manifestation of SOC thresholds relative to biodiversity thresholds required more explicit mechanistic explanation. Our claim is based on the well-documented temporal decoupling between biotic community dynamics and soil carbon cycling. While plant and microbial communities can exhibit rapid compositional shifts in response to N enrichment, driven by changes in species dominance, root exudation, litter quality, and microbial metabolic strategies, these biotic changes do not immediately translate into detectable changes in SOC stocks. This lag arises because SOC accumulation and stabilization are governed by relatively slow, physically and chemically protected processes. In particular, a significant portion of SOC is stabilized through mechanisms such as aggregation, organo-mineral interactions, and chemical recalcitrance, especially in the case of mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC). These pools are inherently resistant to decomposition and have turnover times ranging from decades to millennia. As a result, even when N-induced shifts in plant-microbe communities alter the quantity and quality of organic inputs (e.g., favoring more recalcitrant or labile compounds), the net impact on total SOC may remain undetectable over shorter timescales due to the buffering capacity and inertia of these stable carbon pools. Therefore, while biodiversity thresholds, such as abrupt changes in community composition or functional group dominance, may be detectable early along an N gradient, corresponding SOC thresholds are likely to emerge only after prolonged N exposure, once the system’s capacity to stabilize carbon is overwhelmed. This time-lag effect implies that biodiversity responses may serve as leading indicators of ecosystem change, preceding measurable SOC losses.
To address this issue, we have added further explanation to reflect the time-lagged relationship between community- and carbon-level responses. The revised sentences as:
“However, these microbial shifts may not immediately translate into changes in SOC, particularly in the case of mineral-associated organic carbon (MAOC), which is resistant to rapid turnover49. This temporal lag suggests that biodiversity thresholds, particularly for soil microbes, may precede those of C, potentially delaying detectable SOC destabilization under N enrichment.”. (Line 80-84)
Comment 7: In my previous comment, I raised a question regarding the negative correlation between plant/bacterial diversity and SOC. The revised text provides explanations for the figures but does not address the core issue: why should we expect a negative correlation between microbial diversity and SOC? Does low bacterial diversity truly lead to higher SOC? This still needs further revision.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this important concern. We agree that the negative correlation observed between microbial diversity and SOC requires careful ecological interpretation. The slight negative correlation observed at low N inputs (~<50 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹) reflects a decoupled response of microbial and carbon dynamics rather than a causal relationship. Specifically, microbial diversity may decline due to the negative effects of N enrichment, such as soil acidification, cation toxicity, and nutrient imbalances, while SOC continues to increase primarily due to plant-mediated carbon inputs (e.g., leaf litter and root exudates) driven by competitive interactions among plant species. Thus, this negative correlation does not imply that low microbial diversity directly leads to higher SOC. Instead, it represents a transient, non-causal association where SOC accumulation is primarily governed by plant productivity, whereas microbial communities respond more rapidly to N enrichment due to their high turnover rates.
To clarify, we emphasize that the observed negative correlation between microbial diversity and SOC at low N levels reflects an asynchronous response, where microbial diversity declines due to the negative impacts of N enrichment, while SOC continues to increase due to plant-mediated carbon inputs. This represents a transient, non-causal relationship. The revied sentences as: “The responses of bacterial diversity and SOC showed a slightly negative correlation below ~50 kg N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹ (Fig. 4b), indicating a transient non-causal association. At this stage, the increase in SOC may directly benefit from aboveground productivity (e.g., leaf litter and root exudates)81,82, while the decline in bacterial species may be functionally compensated by redundant taxa83.”. (Line 269-272)
Comment 8: The authors have admitted that many cited papers were incorrect. While these references have been removed, this raises concerns about adherence to proper writing and referencing standards throughout the manuscript.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this important observation. We regret that in earlier drafts, some citations were included with only partial contextual alignment, which may have undermined the manuscript’s scholarly precision. We clarify that these instances involved contextual mismatches rather than factual inaccuracies in the cited works themselves. Nevertheless, we fully acknowledge the importance of rigorous and contextually appropriate referencing.
In response, we have conducted a comprehensive, line-by-line review of all citations in the manuscript. Each reference has been carefully re-evaluated to ensure it is: (1) directly relevant to the claim it supports, (2) accurately interpreted, and (3) drawn from high-quality, peer-reviewed literature. Any citations that did not meet these criteria have been revised or removed. Furthermore, we have meticulously verified that all remaining references adhere strictly to the journal’s formatting guidelines, ensuring consistency and integrity in presentation.
We deeply value the standards of academic integrity and responsible scholarship, and we appreciate the reviewer’s vigilance in upholding them. This feedback has been instrumental in strengthening the overall quality and credibility of our work. We remain fully committed to maintaining the highest standards in scientific writing and citation practices in this submission and in all future research communications.
Comment 9: Regarding the additional meta-regression analysis, the authors claim to have accounted for potential co-variation between effect sizes (lnRRs) by including N rate as a random effect. However, upon reviewing Figure 2f, the results appear unchanged. Which I doubt the results is corrected. Although some results did show significant changes in Fig S3, S4, etc, particularly correlations becoming non-significant. But the authors said that results remained statistically significant. This discrepancy needs clarification, and results should be updated accordingly. Furthermore, it should be clearly indicated in the figure legend that N addition rate was included as a random factor rather than study ID. Overall, the new analysis support my comment that ‘The influence of N addition rates on co-correlations should be treated with caution.’

As noted, we did incorporate N addition rate as a random effect in our meta-regression models to account for the potential co-variation among lnRRs for your previous comment. Upon closer examination of the results in the Fig. 2f, both the regression coefficient and its associated significance level did change after including N rate as a random effect, although the effect size remained in the same direction and the magnitude of the change was modest. We also reviewed and rechecked the results presented in Fig. S3-S5, as previously noted by the reviewer, and indeed observed some degree of change across a few associations after incorporating N addition rate as a random effect. For example, the slope between plant diversity (lnRR) and plant biomass (lnRR) shifted non-significant in Fig. S5, suggesting that N input levels indeed influence co-correlation outcomes, particularly among highly covarying variables. In this study, we aimed to investigate how plant and microbial diversity responses jointly regulate SOC dynamics under varying N enrichment, recognizing that these responses may diverge at certain N input levels and result in ecological trade-offs. However, examining associations between diversity and SOC is challenging, as both may respond to shared N gradients, as you rightly pointed out. While multilevel models can account for some sources of confounding, shared responsiveness to environmental gradients like N input may still introduce statistical co-variation between response variables. Despite this, several pairwise associations were affected by incorporating N addition rate as a random effect, the key analytical results such as the magnitude and direction of variable responses, variable rankings in the random forest model, and the identification of response thresholds along the N gradient, remained unaffected.
